MUSA 5080 | PUBLIC POLICY ANALYTICS

## The Nightmare Begins *Chicago House Price Prediction — Team Research Report* Welcome to **A Nightmare in Regression Class**. This report explores Chicago housing prices through regression modeling, spatial feature engineering, and predictive evaluation. ## Part 0: Setup (provided) These helpers are to help you get off the ground. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(tidycensus) library(sf) library(caret) library(spdep) library(nngeo) library(patchwork) options(scipen = 999) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_na <- function(formula, df) { vars <- all.vars(formula) bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))] if (length(bad) > 0) { stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "), ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).") } } # 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) { df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data check_na(formula, df) set.seed(5080) fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)) fit$results$RMSE } # Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out cv_pred <- function(formula, data) { df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data check_na(formula, df) set.seed(5080) fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, savePredictions = "final")) fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred) } # Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter. socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) { where <- str_squish(where) q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit) if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE)) url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q) tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson") resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e) if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url) st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE) } ``` ::: ### Load both files together (provided) Build every feature on `all_sales`, so training and test houses get identical features. Split off `train` again whenever you add something. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all_sales <- bind_rows( read_csv("data/chicago_train.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(split = "train"), read_csv("data/chicago_test.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(split = "test") ) %>% st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) %>% st_transform(3435) # Illinois East State Plane, feet all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(split) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 split n 1 test 5789 2 train 23200 ``` ::: ::: Useful sources: the [Chicago Data Portal](https://data.cityofchicago.org) (find a dataset's ID under its API button), the Census via `tidycensus`, and Cook County's open data. --- ## Part 1: Clean and explore Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map of price. ### Which sales are market sales? We only remove **training** rows. Every test house is kept and predicted (Rule 1). First we look at how many sales fall in each price band. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train_raw <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") train_raw %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(price_band = cut(sale_price, c(-Inf, 20000, 50000, 100000, Inf), labels = c("< $20k", "$20k–50k", "$50k–100k", "$100k+")), is_multisale) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 8 × 3 price_band is_multisale n 1 < $20k 0 82 2 < $20k 1 1 3 $20k–50k 0 578 4 $20k–50k 1 33 5 $50k–100k 0 1853 6 $50k–100k 1 101 7 $100k+ 0 19455 8 $100k+ 1 1097 ``` ::: ::: The lowest training price is $10,373, so the file already excludes sales under $10,000 (the threshold we used for Philadelphia in class). We add two rules: | # | Rule | Why | Removed | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Drop `is_multisale == 1` | The sale covered more than one parcel, so the price does not describe this one house. Only 196 of these 1,232 sales share a location with another training sale, so the flag marks multi-parcel deals, not houses that sold twice. | 1,232 | | 2 | Drop `sale_price < $20,000` | No single-family house in Chicago sells this cheaply in an arm's-length deal. These are likely family transfers, tax or sheriff sales. | 59 | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train_raw <- train_raw %>% mutate(drop_reason = case_when( is_multisale == 1 ~ "1. Multi-parcel sale", sale_price < 20000 ~ "2. Price under $20,000", TRUE ~ "Kept" )) # Cleaning log: how many rows each rule removed cleaning_log <- train_raw %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(drop_reason, name = "n_rows") %>% mutate(share = scales::percent(n_rows / sum(n_rows), accuracy = 0.1)) cleaning_log ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 drop_reason n_rows share 1 1. Multi-parcel sale 1232 5.3% 2 2. Price under $20,000 59 0.3% 3 Kept 21909 94.4% ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Remove the dropped training rows from all_sales; never touch the test rows keep_ids <- train_raw$id[train_raw$drop_reason == "Kept"] all_sales <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "test" | id %in% keep_ids) all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(split) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 split n 1 test 5789 2 train 21909 ``` ::: ::: The two rules removed 1,291 of 23,200 training sales (5.6%), leaving 21,909. All 5,789 test houses remain. We kept the 527 single-parcel sales between $20,000 and $50,000: a low price alone does not prove a sale is non-market, and similar houses are in the test set. ### Filling missing values Six predictors have missing values, four of them also in the test data. We fill them on `all_sales` with the **median of the cleaned training sales**, so training and test houses are treated the same way. For 0/1 variables, the median is the most common value. Fireplaces have the most missing values (349 in training), so we also add a flag `fireplace_missing`, letting the model learn whether "unknown" differs from the median. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train_tmp <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") %>% st_drop_geometry() all_sales <- all_sales %>% mutate( fireplace_missing = if_else(is.na(num_fireplaces), 1, 0), lotsize_acre = replace_na(lotsize_acre, median(train_tmp$lotsize_acre, na.rm = TRUE)), num_half_baths = replace_na(num_half_baths, median(train_tmp$num_half_baths, na.rm = TRUE)), num_fireplaces = replace_na(num_fireplaces, median(train_tmp$num_fireplaces, na.rm = TRUE)), garage_size = replace_na(garage_size, median(train_tmp$garage_size, na.rm = TRUE)), full_basement = replace_na(full_basement, median(train_tmp$full_basement, na.rm = TRUE)), warmairfurnace = replace_na(warmairfurnace, median(train_tmp$warmairfurnace, na.rm = TRUE)) ) # Check: the only NAs left should be sale_price in the test rows all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>% pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") %>% filter(n_missing > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Spider head annotate( "point", x = spider_x, y = spider_y + 0.065 * yr, shape = 21, size = 4, fill = "#080A09", color = orange, stroke = 0.8 ) + # Spider eyes annotate( "point", x = spider_x + c(-0.035, 0.035), y = spider_y + 0.075 * yr, color = "#F4C76A", size = 1 ) + scale_x_continuous( breaks = seq_len(n_periods), labels = quarterly_prices$period, limits = c(0.5, n_periods + 0.5) ) + scale_y_continuous( labels = scales::label_dollar(), limits = c( max(0, y_min - 0.25 * yr), y_max + 0.85 * yr ) ) + scale_size_continuous( name = "Sales", range = c(3, 7) ) + labs( title = "THE RISE OF THE HAUNTED MARKET", subtitle = "Median Chicago Home Sale Prices | 2023–2025", x = NULL, y = "Median sale price (USD)", caption = "Quarterly median prices | Point size represents number of sales" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme( plot.background = element_rect( fill = bg, color = NA ), panel.background = element_rect( fill = bg, color = NA ), panel.grid.major = element_line( color = "#35413A", linewidth = 0.25 ), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text( color = gold, face = "bold", size = 18 ), plot.subtitle = element_text( color = ivory, size = 11 ), axis.title = element_text( color = gold, face = "bold" ), axis.text = element_text( color = "#E5DCD0" ), axis.text.x = element_text( angle = 45, hjust = 1 ), plot.caption = element_text( color = "#B8A894", size = 9, hjust = 0 ), legend.title = element_text( color = gold ), legend.text = element_text( color = ivory ), legend.background = element_rect( fill = bg, color = NA ), legend.key = element_rect( fill = bg, color = NA ), plot.margin = margin(18, 20, 18, 20) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Median Chicago home sale price by quarter, 2023–2025.](assign5_files/figure-html/fig-price-time-1.png){#fig-price-time width=100%} ::: ::: **Answer:** What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices? *Your answer:* Four things shaped our plan. First, prices are strongly right-skewed: the median cleaned sale is $300,000 but the mean is about $430,000, with a long tail into the millions. Rule 4 keeps the outcome in dollars, so RMSE will be driven by the expensive houses, and we expect our biggest misses there. We can't log the outcome, but we can log skewed predictors. Second, the flexible curves for building size and building age do not follow the straight lines, so we will test `log()` and squared (`I(x^2)`) terms and keep them only if CV RMSE improves. Third, the price map shows that prices cluster by place. A structure-only model will leave spatially clustered errors, and Rule 5 bars features built from neighbors' prices, so we will build location features from open data: tract characteristics from the ACS, distances to amenities, crime exposure (buffer counts and kNN distances), and neighborhood fixed effects. Fourth, the median price rose from $283,000 in 2023 to $310,000 in 2024 and $321,900 in 2025, so sale year and quarter belong in the model as categories. --- ## Part 2: Build the model Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns `model`, `added`, `cv_rmse`, `moran_i`, `notes`. Every model is scored the same way: **10-fold CV RMSE** on the same folds (the provided `cv_rmse()`), and **global Moran's I of the out-of-fold residuals**, using each house's 5 nearest training sales as neighbors. Residual = actual − predicted, so a positive residual means the model guessed too low. A falling Moran's I means the errors are clustering less in space. Rule check for every feature below: nothing is built from a sale price. The Assessor could compute every one of them for a house that did not sell. ### Scoring helpers and the model log ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Spatial weights: each training house's 5 nearest training sales w_knn <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(train), k = 5)), style = "W") # Global Moran's I of a residual vector moran_of <- function(resid) as.numeric(moran.mc(resid, w_knn, nsim = 499)$statistic) # Score one formula: CV RMSE, out-of-fold residuals, Moran's I score_model <- function(f) { resid <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f, train) list(cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f, train), moran_i = moran_of(resid), resid = resid) } model_log <- tibble(model = character(), added = character(), cv_rmse = numeric(), moran_i = numeric(), notes = character()) resids <- list() # out-of-fold residuals of every model, for the Part 3 maps ``` ::: ### M1: Structure-only baseline Every house feature in the file. `fireplace_missing` is the flag from Part 1. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f1 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + lotsize_acre + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths + num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + fireplace_missing + garage_size + central_air + one_story + full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace s1 <- score_model(f1) resids$m1 <- s1$resid model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "m1", added = "structure only (baseline)", cv_rmse = s1$cv_rmse, moran_i = s1$moran_i, notes = "Required baseline: what the house alone can tell us, before any location.") model_log ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 model added cv_rmse moran_i notes 1 m1 structure only (baseline) 281310. 0.376 Required baseline: what the h… ``` ::: ::: ### M2: The shape of building size and lot size In Part 1, the flexible curve for building size did not follow the straight line. We try three shapes and let CV RMSE choose. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f1_log <- update(f1, . ~ . - building_000sf - lotsize_acre + log(building_000sf) + log(lotsize_acre)) f1_sq <- update(f1, . ~ . + I(building_000sf^2)) size_forms <- tibble(form = c("linear (m1)", "log size + log lot", "size + size^2"), f = list(f1, f1_log, f1_sq)) %>% mutate(cv_rmse = map_dbl(f, ~ cv_rmse(.x, train))) %>% arrange(cv_rmse) size_forms %>% select(form, cv_rmse) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 form cv_rmse 1 size + size^2 269783. 2 linear (m1) 281310. 3 log size + log lot 306138. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} f2 <- size_forms$f[[1]] # keep the shape with the lowest CV RMSE s2 <- score_model(f2) resids$m2 <- s2$resid model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "m2", added = paste("size shape:", size_forms$form[1]), cv_rmse = s2$cv_rmse, moran_i = s2$moran_i, notes = "Part 1 scatter bent away from the straight line; compared linear, log and squared size.") ``` ::: ### M3: A squared term for building age The age curve in Part 1 was not a straight line either. Old Chicago houses (greystones, Victorians) can sell for more than mid-century ones, so value may fall with age and then rise again. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f3 <- update(f2, . ~ . + I(building_age^2)) s3 <- score_model(f3) resids$m3 <- s3$resid model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "m3", added = "+ building_age^2", cv_rmse = s3$cv_rmse, moran_i = s3$moran_i, notes = "Age curve bent in Part 1; a squared term lets the line turn.") # Where does the age curve turn? Is it inside the data? m3_fit <- lm(f3, data = st_drop_geometry(train)) b1 <- coef(m3_fit)["building_age"] b2 <- coef(m3_fit)["I(building_age^2)"] c(turning_point = unname(-b1 / (2 * b2)), min_age = min(train$building_age), max_age = max(train$building_age)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` turning_point min_age max_age 84.80734 0.00000 172.00000 ``` ::: ::: ### M4: Sale year and quarter as categories Median prices rose each year (Part 1), and sales may differ by season. Year and quarter are labels, not amounts, so we make them factors. The reference level is 2023, Q1. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all_sales <- all_sales %>% mutate(year_f = factor(year), qrt_f = factor(sale_qrt)) train <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") f4 <- update(f3, . ~ . + year_f + qrt_f) s4 <- score_model(f4) resids$m4 <- s4$resid model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "m4", added = "+ sale year and quarter (factors)", cv_rmse = s4$cv_rmse, moran_i = s4$moran_i, notes = "Median price rose 2023 to 2025 (Part 1); prices also move with season.") ``` ::: ### M5: Distance to the Loop and to the nearest 'L' station The price map in Part 1 shows prices clustering by place. The first two location features: distance to the Loop (City Hall), and distance to the nearest CTA 'L' stop (Chicago Data Portal, dataset `8pix-ypme`). We log both distances, because moving from 500 to 2,500 ft from a station matters more than moving from 20,000 to 22,000 ft. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-87.6319, 41.8837)), crs = 4326) %>% st_transform(3435) cta_stops <- socrata_get("8pix-ypme", where = "location IS NOT NULL") %>% filter(!st_is_empty(.)) %>% st_transform(3435) all_sales <- all_sales %>% mutate( dist_loop_ft = as.numeric(st_distance(., city_hall)), dist_cta_ft = as.numeric(st_distance(., cta_stops[st_nearest_feature(., cta_stops), ], by_element = TRUE)) ) train <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") summary(train$dist_cta_ft) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 120.6 3162.3 6671.0 8324.8 12347.4 36205.6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} f5 <- update(f4, . ~ . + log(dist_loop_ft) + log(dist_cta_ft)) s5 <- score_model(f5) resids$m5 <- s5$resid model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "m5", added = "+ log distance to Loop and to nearest 'L' stop", cv_rmse = s5$cv_rmse, moran_i = s5$moran_i, notes = "Prices cluster by place (Part 1 map); access to downtown and transit is a measurable reason why.") ``` ::: ### M6: Exposure to violent crime Violent crime is a disamenity a buyer cares about and the house file can't see. We pull robberies, homicides, aggravated assaults and aggravated batteries for 2023–2025 (FBI codes 01A, 03, 04A, 04B) from the Chicago Data Portal (`ijzp-q8t2`). Then we build the three ways of operationalizing "near", plus a logged kNN distance, and let CV RMSE pick one. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} violent <- socrata_get( "ijzp-q8t2", where = "date >= '2023-01-01T00:00:00' AND date < '2026-01-01T00:00:00' AND fbi_code IN ('01A', '03', '04A', '04B') AND location IS NOT NULL", select = "id, fbi_code, location" ) %>% filter(!st_is_empty(.)) %>% st_transform(3435) nrow(violent) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 72924 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} violent %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(fbi_code) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fbi_code n 1 01A 1661 2 03 25873 3 04A 22104 4 04B 23286 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all_sales <- all_sales %>% mutate( violent_660ft = lengths(st_intersects(st_buffer(., 660), violent)), # about a block violent_near = as.numeric(st_distance(., violent[st_nearest_feature(., violent), ], by_element = TRUE)), violent_knn5 = sapply(st_nn(., violent, k = 5, returnDist = TRUE, progress = FALSE)$dist, mean) ) train <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") crime_forms <- tibble(feature = c("violent_660ft", "violent_near", "violent_knn5", "log(violent_knn5)")) %>% mutate(f = map(feature, ~ update(f5, as.formula(paste(". ~ . +", .x)))), cv_rmse = map_dbl(f, ~ cv_rmse(.x, train))) %>% arrange(cv_rmse) crime_forms %>% select(feature, cv_rmse) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 feature cv_rmse 1 log(violent_knn5) 240535. 2 violent_660ft 241146. 3 violent_knn5 244719. 4 violent_near 247913. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} f6 <- crime_forms$f[[1]] # keep the version with the lowest CV RMSE s6 <- score_model(f6) resids$m6 <- s6$resid model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "m6", added = paste("+ violent crime:", crime_forms$feature[1]), cv_rmse = s6$cv_rmse, moran_i = s6$moran_i, notes = "Crime is a disamenity the house file can't see; compared buffer count, nearest and kNN.") ``` ::: ### M7: Neighborhood characteristics from the Census Houses in tracts with higher incomes, more college graduates and fewer vacant homes should sell for more, even after distance and crime. We take 2019–2023 ACS 5-year estimates for Cook County tracts and give each house the values of the tract it sits in. Income is skewed, so we log it. A few tracts have no estimate; we fill those with the training median and keep every row (Rule 1). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tracts_acs <- get_acs( geography = "tract", state = "IL", county = "Cook", year = 2023, survey = "acs5", variables = c(med_inc = "B19013_001", # median household income edu_total = "B15003_001", # population 25+ ba = "B15003_022", # bachelor's ma = "B15003_023", # master's prof = "B15003_024", # professional degree phd = "B15003_025", # doctorate hu_total = "B25002_001", # housing units vacant = "B25002_003"), # vacant units output = "wide", geometry = TRUE, progress = FALSE ) %>% st_transform(3435) %>% transmute( tract_GEOID = GEOID, med_inc = med_incE, pct_ba = if_else(edu_totalE > 0, 100 * (baE + maE + profE + phdE) / edu_totalE, NA_real_), pct_vacant = if_else(hu_totalE > 0, 100 * vacantE / hu_totalE, NA_real_) ) n_before <- nrow(all_sales) all_sales <- all_sales %>% st_join(tracts_acs, join = st_nearest_feature) stopifnot(nrow(all_sales) == n_before) # one tract per house # How many houses got a missing estimate? all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% summarise(across(c(med_inc, pct_ba, pct_vacant), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 med_inc pct_ba pct_vacant 1 85 0 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} train_tmp <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") %>% st_drop_geometry() all_sales <- all_sales %>% mutate( med_inc = replace_na(med_inc, median(train_tmp$med_inc, na.rm = TRUE)), pct_ba = replace_na(pct_ba, median(train_tmp$pct_ba, na.rm = TRUE)), pct_vacant = replace_na(pct_vacant, median(train_tmp$pct_vacant, na.rm = TRUE)) ) train <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") f7 <- update(f6, . ~ . + log(med_inc) + pct_ba + pct_vacant) s7 <- score_model(f7) resids$m7 <- s7$resid model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "m7", added = "+ tract log(income), % BA+, % vacant (ACS 2023)", cv_rmse = s7$cv_rmse, moran_i = s7$moran_i, notes = "Neighborhood income, education and vacancy shape demand beyond distance and crime.") ``` ::: ### M8: Community area fixed effects Chicago's 77 community areas each carry things we did not measure: reputation, schools, lake access, history. A fixed effect lets every area have its own intercept. Boundaries come from the Chicago Data Portal (`igwz-8jzy`). A fixed effect can't predict a group it never saw. So before CV we count training sales per area. Areas with fewer than 10 training sales, and any area with only test houses, are merged into the area of the nearest training house in a larger area. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} community_areas <- socrata_get("igwz-8jzy", where = "area_numbe IS NOT NULL", select = "community, area_numbe, the_geom") %>% st_transform(3435) %>% select(community) n_before <- nrow(all_sales) all_sales <- all_sales %>% st_join(community_areas, join = st_nearest_feature) stopifnot(nrow(all_sales) == n_before) # one area per house # Count training sales per area, smallest first ca_counts <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(community) %>% arrange(n) head(ca_counts, 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 2 community n 1 OAKLAND 15 2 WASHINGTON PARK 15 3 FULLER PARK 19 4 ARMOUR SQUARE 31 5 DOUGLAS 38 6 LOWER WEST SIDE 43 7 RIVERDALE 44 8 BURNSIDE 53 9 OHARE 53 10 WEST GARFIELD PARK 56 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Merge small areas (and areas with no training sales) into a neighbor small <- ca_counts %>% filter(n < 10) %>% pull(community) is_small <- all_sales$community %in% small | !(all_sales$community %in% ca_counts$community) donors <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train", !(community %in% small)) nearest <- st_nearest_feature(all_sales[is_small, ], donors) all_sales <- all_sales %>% mutate(community_fe = community) all_sales$community_fe[is_small] <- donors$community[nearest] all_sales <- all_sales %>% mutate(community_fe = factor(community_fe)) train <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") # Check: every group now has at least 10 training sales train %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(community_fe) %>% arrange(n) %>% head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 community_fe n 1 OAKLAND 15 2 WASHINGTON PARK 15 3 FULLER PARK 19 4 ARMOUR SQUARE 31 5 DOUGLAS 38 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} n_distinct(train$community_fe) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 76 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} f8 <- update(f7, . ~ . + community_fe) s8 <- score_model(f8) resids$m8 <- s8$resid model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "m8", added = "+ community area fixed effects (small areas merged)", cv_rmse = s8$cv_rmse, moran_i = s8$moran_i, notes = "Soaks up what is constant about a community area that we did not measure.") ``` ::: ### The model log so far ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model_log ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Use your log. Based on our model log, adding community area fixed effects (M8) produced the largest improvement. CV RMSE decreased from approximately $222,143 in M7 to $196,562 in M8, while residual Moran's I decreased from approximately 0.344 to 0.193. This suggests that neighborhood-level differences explain an important part of Chicago housing prices that our earlier variables did not capture. Adding neighborhood socioeconomic characteristics in M7 also improved prediction substantially. However, the earlier structural and nonlinear features delivered relatively modest improvements, and adding distance-based features did not eliminate spatial clustering. Even our final model retains some spatial autocorrelation, meaning there are still location-specific patterns it cannot fully explain. Overall, the results show that housing prices depend not only on building characteristics but also on the neighborhoods where properties are located. --- ## Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays **4A.** Where does your final model fail worst? Where does the model fail worst? Our final model (M8) has the largest mean absolute prediction errors in Lincoln Park ($504,283), Near North Side ($424,419), and Lake View ($322,603). These neighborhoods contain properties with substantial price variation, which may not be fully captured by our predictors. In Lincoln Park, the model slightly underpredicts sale prices on average, with a mean residual of +$3,451. In Near North Side and Lake View, it slightly overpredicts prices, with mean residuals of -$1,322 and -$1,127, respectively. However, these average errors are relatively small compared with the mean absolute errors, suggesting that large overpredictions and underpredictions often cancel each other out. This shows that community area fixed effects helped improve our model, but they cannot fully capture differences between individual properties, especially in neighborhoods with expensive and diverse housing markets. ### 4B. Does the assessment ratio differ by neighborhood income? Yes. The median predicted-to-actual sale price ratio increases across neighborhood income groups, from 0.971 in the lowest-income neighborhoods to approximately 1.016 in the highest-income neighborhoods. The middle-income groups have median ratios of 0.987 and 0.995. This suggests that our model slightly underpredicts home values in lower-income neighborhoods and slightly overpredicts values in higher-income neighborhoods. At the median, this is different from the regressive assessment pattern discussed in *The Tax Divide*, where lower-income homeowners face a disproportionate tax burden. However, the mean assessment ratios are above 1 across all income groups, with the largest mean ratio in the lowest-income group (1.31). This indicates that some properties experience substantial overprediction, even when the median suggests underprediction. The difference between the mean and median is important when evaluating potential assessment inequities. Our Part 1 cleaning rules excluded multi-parcel sales and transactions below $20,000. While these rules helped remove unusual transactions, they may also affect which properties are represented in our analysis, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods. Finally, these are predictions from our model, not actual property tax assessments. Therefore, we cannot conclude that our model produces the same tax inequities described in *The Tax Divide*. However, the differences across income groups suggest that fairness should be evaluated carefully before using this type of model for property assessment. --- ## Part 5: Predict the test houses (provided) Refit your final recipe on all training sales, then predict every test house. Reading a Coefficient Twice In our final model (M8), the coefficient for `building_000sf` is approximately 175,638.8. Statistically, this means that a one-unit increase in building size, equivalent to 1,000 square feet, is associated with a $175,638.80 increase in predicted sale price, holding all other variables constant. From a prediction perspective, if two houses have identical characteristics except that one is 1,000 square feet larger, our model predicts that the larger house will sell for approximately $175,639 more. This illustrates how structural characteristics directly influence the model's estimated property values. ### 2. Would We Recommend This Model to the Assessor? We would recommend Model 8 as a useful starting point, but not as a fully automated assessment system. Our final cross-validation RMSE was $196,561.80, a substantial improvement over the baseline model. Adding neighborhood fixed effects, census characteristics, crime exposure, and accessibility measures helped capture important differences across Chicago. However, the model still has limitations. The largest mean absolute errors occurred in Lincoln Park ($504,283), Near North Side ($424,419), and Lake View ($322,603). These neighborhoods may contain expensive or unusual properties that are difficult to predict accurately. We also found differences in assessment ratios across neighborhood income groups. The median ratio increased from 0.971 in the lowest-income areas to 1.020 in the highest-income areas. Although this pattern differs from the regressive assessment problem described in *The Tax Divide*, it demonstrates why prediction accuracy and equity should be evaluated together. Before using the model for taxation, we would recommend additional validation, reviewing unusual properties, checking the timing of external data, and regularly monitoring neighborhood-level errors. ### Who Did What | Name | Main Contribution | |---|---| | Alhaylam Alajmi | Data exploration, regression modeling, spatial diagnostics, model evaluation, results interpretation, and report preparation | | Rutong Chen | Data preparation, feature engineering, regression modeling, spatial diagnostics, model evaluation, and report preparation | Both team members collaborated on reviewing the final model, discussing the results, and preparing the team submission. ### AI Team Statement Our team used AI as a supporting tool for coding assistance, debugging, and improving the clarity of written explanations.
